Behavior modification. The application of principles of learning and conditioning to change unwanted behaviors or establish new ones. It is based on the insight that behavior is shaped by its consequences—rewarded behaviors increase, punished behaviors decrease. Behavior modification uses systematic reinforcement and punishment to alter conduct, widely applied in clinical psychology, education, and organizational settings.

B. F. Skinner's work on operant conditioning demonstrated that behavior could be systematically shaped through carefully timed rewards and punishments. This discovery made behavior modification scientifically tractable and practically powerful. Positive reinforcement, rewarding desired behavior, is generally more effective and produces fewer side effects than punishment. Punishment suppresses behavior in the short term but does not teach alternatives and often produces fear and resentment.

Schedules of reinforcement matter greatly. Continuous reinforcement—rewarding every occurrence—builds behavior quickly but extinguishes rapidly once rewards stop. Intermittent reinforcement—rewarding occasional occurrences—produces slower learning but more durable behavior. Token economies use conditioned reinforcers, tokens exchangeable for valued items, to modify behavior in institutional settings, bypassing the need to find universally motivating primary reinforcers.

Extinction—withdrawing reinforcement from a previously reinforced behavior—can eliminate unwanted behaviors, but it often produces an initial extinction burst, a temporary increase in the unwanted behavior as the organism tries harder. Shaping, reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior, allows modification of complex behaviors that rarely occur naturally. The organism is gradually guided toward the desired endpoint through incremental rewards.

Self-monitoring and self-reinforcement allow individuals to modify their own behavior. Awareness of behavioral patterns and deliberate self-reward can change habits without external intervention. Behavior modification raises ethical concerns. Applied coercively in prisons or without consent, it can become a tool of control. Applied therapeutically to help people overcome phobias, it liberates. The same method serves both freedom and domination.
